newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASEAN-EU ties grow despite split on Burma, Timor.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN-EU ties grow despite split on Burma, Timor.

text.p: European and Southeast Asian nations have agreed on new programmes to expand ties at a meeting overshadowed by robust exchanges on Burma, East Timor and human rights, officials said on Friday.

Foreign ministers from the European Union (EU) and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) were to issue a Final Declaration on Friday outlining fresh ways to take economic, political and cultural ties to a new level.
But much of the discussion at their inter-regional meeting has been on subjects scarely mentioned in the 16-page declaration -- Burma, East Timor and the sensitive subject of human rights.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said on Thursday: "There are many things that bind us, many things that we have made progress on ... On the other hand, there are -- and I want to be frank about it -- also things on which we disagree."
The 22 foreign ministers spent more than two hours talking about Burma on Thursday, but the declaration simply says on the subject: "We had an exchange of views on Myanmar (Burma)."
Still, Burma got more of a mention than East Timor, which, to Jakarta's satisfaction, doesn't appear at all in the declaration.

The meeting's co-chairman, Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar, said of the Burma discussions: "This was one of the most productive and substantive discussions between the EU and ASEAN held to date.

"Not that each side has convinced the other," he said. "But both sides agreed that we now have, as a result of the dialogue, a better understanding of each other's insights, concerns and approaches on Myanmar."

The EU believes tough measures are needed to punish the Rangoon government for its crackdown on Burma's pro-democracy movement, while ASEAN believes "constructive engagement" will eventually coax the military rulers to reform.

Indonesia annexed East Timor in 1976 in a civil war that erupted after Portugal's abrupt decolonisation. A third of the population died in the famine and fighting that followed. The United Nations still considers Portugal the administering power.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas on Thursday accused Portugal of scuttling an ambitious treaty that would redefine ties between ASEAN and the EU into the next century.
"(East Timor) was one of the issues used by Portugal to prevent a new-generation agreement to be signed by the two sides and of course we deeply regret it," Alatas told reporters.
Portugal's Foreign Minister Jaime Gama said Lisbon had not vetoed the treaty, but was merely insisting that political and human rights issues be included.
Countries that did not want to include human rights issues in the treaty "are the ones who are putting the veto" on a new agreement, he told reporters.
The old ASEAN-EU agreement was signed in 1980, when ties were largely defined by aid from European nations to some of their former colonies in Asia.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. All but Thailand are former European colonies.
A new agreement would outline dozens of new initiatives across the political, economic and cultural spectrum.
A senior ASEAN official said because it would have treaty status it needs to be signed by all members -- something Portugal has declined to do in its present form.
The official said, however, many of the projects envisaged for the treaty would be included in the final declaration from this week's ministerial meeting.
